summary: This work demonstrates that an all-fluxonium cross-resonance (CR) architecture with only direct capacitive coupling can achieve CNOT gate durations under 200 ns with residual ZZ rates of 50 kHz, using a semi-analytical approach that combines numerical Floquet diagonalization with perturbative two-qubit coupling. Detailed frequency-collision analysis and Monte Carlo simulations show that the high anharmonicity of fluxoniums enables substantially improved scalability compared to transmons, requiring only ~1–2% Josephson-energy disorder to maintain >50% collision-free yield for surface codes up to distance 21.
motivation: Transmon-based CR architectures face severe frequency-collision limitations that restrict scaling beyond ~1000 qubits even with sophisticated fabrication control, motivating exploration of higher-anharmonicity alternatives like fluxoniums to enable practical multi-qubit processors with fixed capacitive couplings and microwave-activated gates.
method: For driven control and idle target fluxoniums coupled via $J n_c \otimes n_t$, the authors (1) numerically diagonalize the Floquet Hamiltonian of the strongly-driven control qubit, (2) perturbatively incorporate the weak coupling to extract effective two-qubit interaction coefficients including the conditional polarization $\Delta p(\Omega)$, (3) derive collision windows via semiclassical transition-rate analysis, and (4) run Monte Carlo simulations sampling junction disorder to predict collision-free yields on square, hexagonal, and heavy-hex lattices.
result: For control qubits at $\omega_c/2\pi \approx 286$ MHz and targets spanning 422–920 MHz with $|\mu_{ZZ}|/2\pi = 50$ kHz, $\tau_{CNOT}^\star \approx \pi/(2J|n_c^{10}n_t^{10}|)$ yields gates in 130–230 ns depending on Josephson-energy ratios; a distance-21 heavy-hexagon surface code achieves >50% zero-collision yield for $\sigma(E_J)/\langle E_J \rangle < 2\%$, versus <1% for transmons at the same disorder.
